sectionAlpha.title: UX Laws & Principles
sectionAlpha.subtitle: Essential user experience laws and principles that guide effective product design and user interaction.

cards.title: Peak-End Rule
cards.shortDescription: Users' recollection of their experience is heavily influenced by the most intense point and the end of the experience, which should be considered when evaluating feedback.

cards.title: Law of Validation
cards.shortDescription: Assumptions must be validated with real user data to avoid building the wrong product.

cards.title: Law of Divergence and Convergence
cards.shortDescription: Effective discovery involves exploring a wide range of ideas (divergence) and then selecting the most promising ones (convergence).

cards.title: Law of Technical Debt
cards.shortDescription: Unaddressed technical debt accumulates interest, making future changes more costly and time-consuming.

cards.title: Law of Customer Retention
cards.shortDescription: Retaining existing customers is more cost-effective than acquiring new ones, so operations should focus on customer satisfaction and loyalty.

cards.title: Law of Feedback Loops
cards.shortDescription: Short feedback loops enable faster learning and improvement in product operations.

cards.title: Brooks's Law
cards.shortDescription: Adding more resources to a late project will delay it further due to increased communication overhead.

cards.title: Iron Triangle Law
cards.shortDescription: In product delivery, you can fix two of the three constraints—scope, time, and cost—but the third must be flexible.

cards.title: Law of Early Testing
cards.shortDescription: Defects found early in the development process are cheaper to fix than those found later.

cards.title: Aesthetic-Usability Effect
cards.shortDescription: Users often perceive aesthetically pleasing design as design that's more usable.

cards.title: Doherty Threshold
cards.shortDescription: Productivity soars when a computer and its users interact at a pace (<400ms) that ensures that neither has to wait on the other.

cards.title: Fitt's Law
cards.shortDescription: The time to acquire a target is a function of the distance to and size of the target.

cards.title: Hick's Law
cards.shortDescription: The time it takes to make a decision increases with the number and complexity of choices.

cards.title: Jakob's Law
cards.shortDescription: Users spend most of their time on other sites. This means that users prefer your site to work the same way as all the other sites they already know.

cards.title: Law of Common Region
cards.shortDescription: Elements tend to be perceived into groups if they are sharing an area with a clearly defined boundary.

cards.title: Law of Proximity
cards.shortDescription: Objects that are near, or proximate to each other, tend to be grouped together.

cards.title: Parkinson's Law
cards.shortDescription: Any task will inflate until all of the available time is spent.

peak-end-rule.title: Peak-End Rule
peak-end-rule.overview: The Peak-End Rule states that people judge an experience largely based on how they felt at its peak and at its end, rather than the total sum or average of every moment of the experience. This cognitive bias significantly impacts how users remember and evaluate their interactions with products.
keyPrinciples: Peak moments create lasting impressions that outweigh the overall experience
The ending of an experience has disproportionate impact on memory
Duration neglect means users don't accurately remember how long experiences lasted
Positive peaks and endings can overcome negative aspects of the journey
applicationInPM: Design onboarding flows that end on a high note with early wins
Create peak moments of delight throughout the user journey
Ensure customer support interactions conclude positively
Plan product launches with memorable peaks and strong conclusions
Use the rule when collecting user feedback - timing matters
examples: Netflix ending episodes on cliffhangers to create positive anticipation
Uber's thank you message and trip summary after rides
Slack's celebratory animations when teams reach milestones
Apple's unboxing experience designed as a peak moment
commonMistakes: Focusing only on averages when measuring user satisfaction
Neglecting the importance of how experiences conclude
Creating peaks too early in the journey without strong endings
Assuming users accurately remember the duration of experiences

law-of-validation.title: Law of Validation
law-of-validation.overview: The Law of Validation emphasizes that assumptions must be validated with real user data and evidence before making significant product decisions. This principle helps product managers avoid building features or products that users don't actually want or need.
keyPrinciples: Assumptions are hypotheses that need testing, not facts
User behavior often differs from what users say they'll do
Early validation saves time and resources
Multiple validation methods provide stronger evidence
applicationInPM: Create testable hypotheses for all major product decisions
Use prototypes and MVPs to validate concepts quickly
Conduct user interviews and usability testing
Analyze user behavior data and metrics
A/B test features before full rollout
examples: Dropbox's video prototype that validated demand before building the product
Buffer's landing page experiment to test interest in their scheduling tool
Zappos' initial model of manually fulfilling orders to validate the online shoe market
Instagram's focus on photo-sharing after validating that users loved the photo features of Burbn
commonMistakes: Confusing validation with confirmation bias
Only validating with internal stakeholders
Asking users what they want instead of observing what they do
Skipping validation for 'obvious' features

aesthetic-usability-effect.title: Aesthetic-Usability Effect
aesthetic-usability-effect.overview: The Aesthetic-Usability Effect describes the tendency for users to perceive more aesthetically pleasing designs as easier to use, even when they are not necessarily more functional. This cognitive bias significantly impacts user perceptions and tolerance for usability issues.
keyPrinciples: Visual appeal influences perceived usability
Users are more tolerant of minor usability issues in attractive interfaces
First impressions matter significantly
Aesthetic design creates positive emotional responses
applicationInPM: Invest in visual design alongside functionality
Ensure consistent visual language across the product
Prioritize the design of key user touchpoints
Use aesthetics to build trust and credibility
examples: Apple's products being perceived as more intuitive due to their design
Airbnb's focus on beautiful photography improving perceived ease of use
Stripe's clean design making payment processing feel more trustworthy
Notion's aesthetic interface making complex functionality feel approachable
commonMistakes: Prioritizing aesthetics over actual usability
Assuming good looks can fix fundamental usability problems
Neglecting accessibility in pursuit of beauty
Creating designs that look good but are hard to use

product-vision-canvas.title: Product Vision Canvas
product-vision-canvas.overview: The Product Vision Canvas is a strategic tool that helps product teams align on the product vision, target users, and business goals. It provides a structured way to articulate and communicate the product strategy.
keyPrinciples: Clear vision drives better decision-making
Alignment reduces wasted effort
Visual representation aids understanding
Regular revision keeps strategy current
applicationInPM: Onboard new team members with the canvas
examples: Tesla's vision of sustainable transport informing all product decisions
Spotify's vision of giving everyone access to music guiding feature development
Slack's vision of making work simpler and more productive
commonMistakes: Creating visions that are too vague or generic
Setting and forgetting the vision
Not involving the whole team in vision creation
Confusing vision with features

business-model-canvas.title: Business Model Canvas
business-model-canvas.overview: The Business Model Canvas is a visual framework for developing, documenting, and understanding business models. It breaks down a business model into nine essential components.
keyPrinciples: Visual representation simplifies complex business models
Nine key components cover all aspects of business
Iterative design enables business model evolution
Shared understanding among stakeholders
examples: Netflix's evolution from DVD rental to streaming platform
Uber's platform business model connecting riders and drivers
Freemium models like Spotify or Dropbox
commonMistakes: Treating the canvas as a one-time exercise
Not validating key assumptions
Focusing too much on the tool rather than insights
Neglecting external market forces

rice-scoring.title: RICE Scoring
rice-scoring.overview: RICE is a prioritization framework that evaluates initiatives based on four criteria: Reach (how many users), Impact (effect on users), Confidence (certainty of estimates), and Effort (resources required).
keyPrinciples: Quantitative approach reduces bias in prioritization
Four dimensions provide comprehensive evaluation
Scoring enables comparison across different types of initiatives
Regular re-evaluation keeps priorities current
applicationInPM: Compare initiatives across different product areas
examples: Prioritizing new features vs. technical improvements
Comparing user acquisition vs. retention initiatives
Evaluating platform expansion opportunities
commonMistakes: Using precise numbers for inherently uncertain estimates
Not updating scores as new information becomes available
Ignoring strategic initiatives that don't score well
Over-relying on the framework without considering context

jobs-to-be-done.title: Jobs-to-be-Done
jobs-to-be-done.overview: Jobs-to-be-Done is a framework for understanding the underlying motivations behind customer behavior by focusing on the 'job' customers are trying to accomplish when they use a product.
keyPrinciples: Customers hire products to do specific jobs
Jobs are functional, emotional, and social
Competition is anything that solves the same job
Innovation opportunities exist in job satisfaction gaps
examples: Netflix helping people 'kill time' and 'be entertained'
Uber solving the job of 'getting from A to B quickly'
Instagram helping people 'share moments' and 'stay connected'
commonMistakes: Confusing jobs with features or solutions
Focusing only on functional jobs, ignoring emotional/social aspects
Not identifying the complete job story
Assuming all customers have the same job

design-thinking.title: Design Thinking
design-thinking.overview: Design Thinking is a human-centered approach to innovation that integrates the needs of people, the possibilities of technology, and requirements for business success.
keyPrinciples: Human-centered approach puts users first
Iterative process enables continuous learning
Collaborative methodology involves diverse perspectives
Prototype early and often to validate ideas
applicationInPM: Discover unmet user needs through empathy
Implement solutions based on user feedback
examples: Airbnb's focus on host and guest experience design
IDEO's approach to product innovation
Google's user-centered design process
commonMistakes: Rushing through the empathy phase
Not involving actual users in the process
Creating prototypes that are too polished for testing
Treating it as a linear rather than iterative process

supply-demand.title: Supply and Demand
supply-demand.overview: Supply and demand is a fundamental economic model that explains how prices are determined in a market economy. For product managers, understanding this model helps in pricing decisions, market analysis, and predicting user behavior.
keyPrinciples: Price is determined by the intersection of supply and demand
Scarcity increases value
Market equilibrium is dynamic
External factors can shift supply and demand curves
examples: Surge pricing in ride-sharing apps during high demand
Limited edition product releases creating artificial scarcity
Freemium models balancing free supply with paid demand
Platform marketplaces managing supply and demand sides
commonMistakes: Ignoring demand when increasing supply
Assuming infinite demand for quality products
Not considering substitute products
Misunderstanding price elasticity

opportunity-cost.title: Opportunity Cost
opportunity-cost.overview: Opportunity cost represents the value of the best alternative forgone when making a choice. For product managers, this concept is crucial for resource allocation and prioritization decisions.
keyPrinciples: Every choice involves giving up alternatives
True cost includes both explicit and implicit costs
Resources are finite and require trade-offs
Optimal decisions consider all alternatives
applicationInPM: Technical debt vs new feature decisions
examples: Choosing to build new features instead of improving performance
Hiring engineers vs marketers with limited budget
Entering new markets vs deepening existing ones
Building in-house vs buying third-party solutions
commonMistakes: Only considering obvious costs, ignoring hidden ones
Not quantifying the value of alternatives
Making decisions without considering trade-offs
Focusing on sunk costs instead of future opportunities

first-principles.title: First Principles Thinking
first-principles.overview: First principles thinking involves breaking down complex problems into their most fundamental truths and building up solutions from there, rather than reasoning by analogy.
keyPrinciples: Question assumptions and conventional wisdom
Break problems down to fundamental truths
Build solutions from the ground up
Challenge existing paradigms
applicationInPM: Reimagining product categories and user experiences
examples: Tesla reimagining cars as computers on wheels
Uber questioning the need for taxi medallions
Netflix moving from physical to digital distribution
Stripe simplifying online payments from first principles
commonMistakes: Accepting industry conventions without question
Reasoning purely by analogy to existing solutions
Not digging deep enough into fundamental truths
Ignoring practical constraints when rebuilding

systems-thinking.title: Systems Thinking
systems-thinking.overview: Systems thinking is a holistic approach to analysis that focuses on the way that a system's constituent parts interrelate and how systems work over time and within the context of larger systems.
keyPrinciples: The whole is greater than the sum of its parts
Structure drives behavior
Systems have purpose and function
Causality is circular, not linear
examples: Apple's ecosystem of interconnected devices and services
Amazon's flywheel effect connecting customers, selection, and experience
Platform businesses creating network effects
Freemium models where free users attract paid users
commonMistakes: Optimizing parts without considering the whole system
Ignoring feedback loops and delayed effects
Focusing on events rather than underlying patterns
Not considering system boundaries and environment

cognitive-biases.title: Cognitive Biases
cognitive-biases.overview: Cognitive biases are systematic errors in thinking that affect the decisions and judgments that people make. Understanding these biases helps product managers make better decisions and design better user experiences.
keyPrinciples: Human thinking is systematically flawed
Biases affect both users and product teams
Awareness can help mitigate bias effects
Design can either exploit or counteract biases
applicationInPM: Designing user interfaces that account for user biases
Making better product decisions by recognizing team biases
Creating ethical persuasion in product design
examples: Confirmation bias affecting user research interpretation
Anchoring bias influencing pricing perception
Loss aversion driving freemium conversion strategies
Social proof in user onboarding and testimonials
commonMistakes: Assuming rational user behavior
Not recognizing own biases in decision-making
Exploiting biases unethically
Ignoring cultural differences in bias expression
